narrative: Your application was denied because the model estimated an 84.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, this reflects a high predicted risk rather than a judgment that you cannot succeed. The strongest factor driving that risk was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest tenth of your class, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. The second strongest factor was your first-year class standing, also in the lowest tenth and well below the accepted-student average. Those two academic signals together pushed the prediction strongly toward failure, and because they concern sustained classroom performance they carried more weight than your LSAT. Your LSAT score of 40 was above the accepted-student average of about 37 and was the third most influential factor, but it worked in your favor and was not enough to offset the class-standing concerns. To move forward, ask admissions for specific feedback, consider delaying enrollment while you strengthen your academic record through additional coursework or a structured study plan, and seek advising on schools or pathways with holistic review. Provide context for your early grades if there were exceptional circumstances, and ask what evidence would let them reconsider your readiness.
